When command syntax, path semantics, launcher behavior, or agent/tool availability depends on execution context, record the terminal surface/host, actual shell/interpreter, kernel/OS/runtime boundary, execution target (local, WSL, container, VM, SSH/remote, or CI), and material path/filesystem semantics. A terminal application is not the shell, and a shell prompt does not prove the kernel/runtime or target. If these facts materially affect the next mutation and cannot be recovered, set `EXECUTION_CONTEXT=UNKNOWN` and do not emit a guessed shell-specific or target-specific write command. If host and target differ, route/handoff or use an explicitly target-scoped invocation.

5B. DEVELOPMENT MUTATION VS ACTIVE PRODUCTION USE
Production/use path is a consumer path, not the default development mutation target. Record `PROD_USE_STATE` as ACTIVE, QUIESCED, OFFLINE, or UNKNOWN from current evidence. ACTIVE includes a process, service, launcher, server/watcher, scheduled job, sync/updater, operator session, or other consumer that can observe the path. UNKNOWN is not idle: it blocks production-path mutation while safe development work may continue.
- When development and production are separate, edit/build/test only in the canonical development checkout or approved worktree, then cross the tracked sync/install/update/promotion boundary. Do not copy a partially built tree into production or use ad-hoc file edits as deployment.
- When development and production resolve to the same physical path, record that relation explicitly. Any write is production-impacting; do not call it a dev-only change. Either the tracked contract must prove in-place mutation is safe for the current use state, or isolate development before changing files.
- Do not `git pull`, reset, rebuild, overwrite, or regenerate files in an ACTIVE production/use path merely because it is local. When consumers could observe files mid-update, use the repository-native safe boundary: quiescence, staged/atomic or versioned replacement, restart/reload coordination, or an equivalent mechanism that prevents partial candidate state. Do not invent a deployment mechanism when the repository already owns one.
- After promotion/update, resolve the production version from the real entrypoint and preserve the repository-defined restore/rollback path when the update can fail after mutation.

6. FAIL CLOSED ON PATH DRIFT
When identity matters, a mismatch must report canonical rule/path, observed path, attempted role, evidence source, and exact safe next action. Use CANONICAL + PROVED, NONCANONICAL + PRESERVE, NONCANONICAL + DISPOSABLE, MISSING, CONFLICT, or UNKNOWN. UNKNOWN is not permission to guess.

7. REMOTE INTEGRATION IS NOT LOCAL DEPLOYMENT
Track separately:
- REMOTE_INTEGRATED — intended commit is contained in refreshed remote default branch.
- DEV_CHECKOUT_CURRENT — canonical development checkout contains the required integrated commit and is safely reconciled.
- PROD_PATH_CURRENT — canonical production/use path consumed the required version through its real mechanism.
- ENTRYPOINT_PROVED — real operator entrypoint resolves the canonical production path and observes intended behavior.
A GitHub merge proves only remote integration. Updating the dev checkout does not prove a separate install/use path was refreshed.

8. MAP BOTH PATHS WHEN TEST PROOF IS INVOLVED
After location identity is proved, compare:
A. REAL: operator action -> canonical production/use path -> launcher/wrapper -> shell/interpreter -> config/environment -> services/native boundaries -> result.
B. TEST: test runner -> checkout/fixture/helper -> exercised boundaries -> assertions.
Mark material boundaries SAME + PROVED, SAME + WEAKER INPUT, SIMULATED/MOCKED, BYPASSED, PRODUCTION-ONLY, or UNKNOWN. Green helper tests do not prove a production wrapper, installed copy, or workstation path they never invoked. Use same-entrypoint synthetic proof when live execution is unavailable but the real launcher can be exercised safely.

9. SECOND PASS — TRY TO CREATE THE BUG AGAIN
Ask:
- Could another agent entering fresh still choose a different directory?
- Could OS/user/home, Desktop Known Folder, OneDrive redirection, mount/junction, or profile state make the same logical rule resolve differently?
- Could a launcher use a stale install while remote main/dev checkout are current?
- Could an ACTIVE or UNKNOWN production consumer observe files while development, sync, build, or update mutates its path?
- Could development and production resolve to the same physical directory so a supposedly dev-only write is actually live?
- Could the terminal host mask a different shell, kernel/runtime, execution target, or path semantics and make the next command wrong?
- Could a parallel agent create a second mutable checkout?
- Could a mirror/cache/backup be mistaken for source authority?
- Could a resolver silently fall back when canonical evidence is missing?
Add the smallest practical regression for concrete gaps; stop at a bounded fixed point.

10. DELIVER
Report the PATH INPUT RECEIPT/resolution source; material EXECUTION CONTEXT RECEIPT; PROD_USE_STATE; canonical development/use/worktree paths and their physical relation; owning contract/resolver and dev-to-production promotion/update boundary; noncanonical-copy disposition; remote SHA; local/prod/entrypoint proof; files/commit/PR/integration state; and exact blocker for any uninspected machine.

CLOSURE RULE
Close only when future agents/operators can derive the same development and production locations from repository-owned evidence, environment-dependent literals resolve reproducibly without hard-coded usernames, path drift is blocked or diagnosed, unique work is preserved, ordinary mutation stays in development unless a same-path production-safe contract is proved, active production cannot observe partial candidate state, and remote integration is no longer confused with local deployment.

prompts.name: Use-Case Closure Certification
prompts.sprintRole: Reconstruct a user-facing closure claim into acceptance obligations, try to falsify it, repair exposed gaps, and certify only evidence-backed closure
prompts.useWhen: A feature, workflow, deployment, or operator use case is being called done/working/closed and the claim needs adversarial acceptance proof rather than a completion summary.
prompts.inspectFirst: The original user-facing request and closure claim; current implementation and entrypoints; acceptance criteria; tests/validators; generated artifacts; known incidents; first-run/repeat-run/failure/upgrade/context variants; integration and runtime evidence. For agent-authored claims, recover the relevant information available to the generating agent so missing-context factuality can be separated from present-but-ignored faithfulness.
prompts.expectedOutput: A reconstructed closure claim, obligation ledger with PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN/NOT-APPLICABLE states, adversarial falsification attempts, repaired in-scope gaps, rerun proof, and an exact certified proof level or reason closure remains open. When an agent-generated claim misses source truth, include a factuality/faithfulness/attention classification and the matched repair.
prompts.nextStep: Translate the user-facing claim into concrete observable obligations, mark current evidence without treating unknown as pass, attack the weakest obligation, repair any exposed gap, and repeat until the claim survives the bounded falsification pass.
prompts.proofGate: Every material obligation implied by the claimed use case is explicit and evidence-linked; UNKNOWN is not PASS; at least one deliberate falsification pass covers practical first-run/repeat/failure/upgrade/context variants; exposed in-scope gaps are repaired and revalidated; and certification states the exact proof level without inflating static or synthetic evidence into live closure. A material contradiction or omission of authoritative information already available in generation context is a faithfulness hallucination and reopens closure; do not repair it by blindly adding more context.
prompts.copyContent:
CERTIFY THE USER-FACING USE CASE. TRY TO PROVE THE CLOSURE CLAIM FALSE BEFORE CALLING IT CLOSED.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Use case / original request: xyz_use_case
Claim being certified: xyz_done_working_closed_claim

MISSION
Turn a vague completion claim into observable acceptance obligations. Gather current evidence, mark gaps honestly, attack the weakest assumptions, repair exposed in-scope defects, and certify only the proof level that survives a deliberate falsification pass. This is user-facing closure certification, not merely a clean PR or a polished final report.

1. RECONSTRUCT THE CLAIM
Recover what the user actually expects to be able to do. Translate `works`, `done`, `deployed`, `fixed`, or equivalent language into concrete observable obligations: entrypoint, inputs, outputs, state changes, failure behavior, persistence, permissions/context, compatibility, restore/cleanup behavior, and any explicit no-regression constraints.
Do not add requirements the request never implied. Do not drop inconvenient requirements because implementation already exists.

2. BUILD THE OBLIGATION LEDGER
For each material obligation record:
- obligation;
- owning surface;
- evidence;
- status: PASS / FAIL / UNKNOWN / NOT APPLICABLE;
- proof level;
- next falsification or repair action.
UNKNOWN is not PASS. `No known bug` is not evidence. A merged PR proves integration, not necessarily the operator use case.

2A. CHECK FAITHFULNESS BEFORE FETCHING MORE
When an agent authored the claim, pin the authoritative truth and the relevant generation context when recoverable. Classify a material mismatch as FACTUALITY_MISSING_CONTEXT (needed truth absent), FAITHFULNESS_CONTEXT_IGNORED (truth/instruction present but ignored, contradicted, or materially underused), ATTENTION_SATURATION (required truth present inside distracting/overgrown context), MIXED, or UNKNOWN.
A confident, plausible, good-faith answer can still fail closure. Missing context calls for targeted retrieval/grounding. If the correct information was already available, do not reflexively add more context: re-anchor to the smallest authoritative sources, compact stale/distracting material, rebuild the affected obligations, and rerun certification.


3. FALSIFY CLOSURE
Choose the weakest or highest-consequence obligations first. Exercise practical variants such as:
- first run vs repeat run;
- ordinary success vs meaningful failure;
- empty/malformed/partial input when relevant;
- old state -> new state/upgrade;
- alternate supported shell/platform/user/privilege context;
- stale state/cache/configuration;
- interruption/retry/idempotency;
- cleanup/restore;
- real launcher/entrypoint vs helper path.
Use only variants relevant to the claim. Do not create ceremonial test volume.

4. REOPEN ON EVIDENCE
If a falsification attempt fails, closure is open. Repair the smallest canonical owner, add a regression where practical, rerun affected obligations, and update the ledger. Do not preserve a green status by weakening an acceptance obligation.

5. SECOND PASS
After all material obligations are green at the claimed level, critique the ledger once more: `What could make the user reasonably say this is not actually closed?` Inspect current diff, tests, artifacts, runtime path, and known failure classes. Close concrete in-scope gaps immediately. Stop only at a bounded fixed point.

6. PROOF LEVEL
Separate: static/schema, unit/helper, integration, same-entrypoint synthetic, field/live runtime, and user-observed acceptance where those levels exist. State the ceiling. Never call synthetic proof live closure.

7. AUTONOMY
Perform repository inspection, safe tests, artifact checks, and repairs yourself. Do not ask the user to validate what the agent can verify. Ask for user participation only when closure truly depends on inaccessible credentials/runtime, physical action, explicit consent, or irreducible user-observed acceptance.

DELIVER
Claim; obligation ledger; falsification passes; gaps found and repaired; validators/tests/runtime checks; evidence still UNKNOWN; certified proof level/ceiling; commit/PR/integration state; exact blocker if closure remains open.

CERTIFICATION RULE
`CLOSED` is valid only when every material obligation is PASS or evidence-backed NOT APPLICABLE at the declared proof level and the deliberate falsification pass exposes no practical unaddressed gap. Otherwise report `NOT CERTIFIED` and continue repair when safe.

prompts.name: Regression Test & Live Behavior Guard
prompts.sprintRole: Prove that a change preserves previously accepted behavior while adding or repairing the requested behavior, using impact-guided automated regressions plus canonical live tests when the claim is runtime-facing
prompts.useWhen: A code, configuration, migration, refactor, bug fix, or feature change may break behavior that previously worked, especially when agents are tempted to validate only the new happy path or the tests they just edited.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current default-branch fixed point; exact changed head/diff; original user outcome and prior accepted behavior; existing tests and runtime evidence; callers/call stacks/interfaces/contracts/state boundaries touched by the change; incidents and regressions; canonical launchers/entrypoints; safe live-test environment and proof limits. For interactive products, inspect multi-step keyboard/pointer sequences and the ownership of search, filters, focus, selection, panel, clipboard, notification, and preference state rather than testing each control in isolation.
prompts.expectedOutput: A protected-behavior ledger, change-impact/call-stack map, before/after regression evidence, new and existing automated tests, canonical live behavior proof when safely available, repaired regressions, deliberate second-pass review, and an honest proof ceiling for any runtime that cannot be exercised. For UI changes, include sequence-level controls proving orthogonal state survives unrelated actions and that a repaired shortcut reaches its intended terminal action without creating a new redundant interaction.
prompts.nextStep: Pin the known-good fixed point and changed head, derive the smallest protected-behavior set from accepted behavior and impacted call stacks, run baseline/current tests plus the canonical live path where safe, repair any regression without weakening the old contract, then rerun both old and new behavior through a second pass.
prompts.proofGate: Previously accepted behavior is explicit rather than inferred from the changed tests alone; impacted callers/call stacks and state/contracts are inspected; expected outputs are not rewritten merely to bless a regression; both requested behavior and protected controls pass; runtime-facing claims receive canonical live proof when safely executable or an exact runtime blocker/proof ceiling; and a deliberate second pass finds no practical untested regression surface in scope. Interactive regressions include realistic action sequences: controls preserve state they do not semantically own, and keyboard/pointer routes that mean the same thing converge on equivalent observable results.
prompts.copyContent:
PROVE THIS CHANGE DID NOT BREAK BEHAVIOR THAT ALREADY WORKED. TEST THE NEW OUTCOME AND THE PROTECTED OLD OUTCOMES; DO NOT VALIDATE ONLY THE PATH YOU JUST CHANGED.

Repo: xyz_repo_or_path
Change / PR / commit: xyz_change_identity
Requested outcome: xyz_new_or_repaired_behavior
Known-good reference: resolve current accepted main/release/commit from evidence

MISSION
Treat regression testing as preservation proof. Establish what was already expected to keep working, determine which call stacks/contracts/state transitions the change can affect, exercise the smallest meaningful protected set before and after the change when practical, and repair any breakage without weakening the old contract just to make tests green. For runtime-facing use cases, run the canonical live path yourself when a safe environment is available.

1. PIN THE COMPARISON FLOOR
- Refresh repository/provider truth and identify the exact known-good reference and exact candidate head.
- Preserve versioned evidence: a test or live run proves only the head, inputs, environment, and entrypoint it actually observed.
- If the reference itself is already broken or ambiguous, say so and use the strongest earlier accepted evidence rather than fabricating a baseline.

2. BUILD THE PROTECTED-BEHAVIOR LEDGER
Recover behavior that the change must preserve from:
- the original/current user request and explicit non-regression constraints;
- existing focused/integration/end-to-end tests that represent real contracts;
- prior accepted runtime/field evidence, runbooks, examples, bug history, and compatibility promises;
- observable behavior at interfaces touched by the diff.
For each protected behavior record: entrypoint, input/state, expected observable result, owning contract/test, proof level, and why the current change could affect it.
Do not assume every existing test is a valuable contract. Do not let deleting or rewriting a test silently delete an accepted behavior.

3. TRACE CHANGE IMPACT THROUGH CALL STACKS
Inspect the changed symbols/files and map practical affected paths:
ENTRYPOINT -> CALLER -> ORCHESTRATION -> DOMAIN/STATE OWNER -> ADAPTER/IO -> RESULT/ERROR.
Include reverse callers and shared dependencies, schema/config migrations, caches/state, retries/cleanup, privilege/context, serialization, and concurrency only when the diff can reach them.
Use this map to select regressions. Do not run an enormous unrelated suite as a substitute for understanding impact.

3A. PROTECT COMPOSED UI STATE AND INTERACTION SEQUENCES
For interactive products, a set of individually passing controls can still form a broken journey. Add sequence-level protected controls around state that composes across actions: search query/results, active filters, focus, selection, detail/panel visibility, clipboard/completion feedback, and persisted preferences where relevant. For each action, name the state it semantically owns and the state it must leave untouched.

A visibility toggle should not erase an active search query or its matching result set unless clearing search is an explicit product contract. Likewise, a shortcut that is meant to complete a user action must be tested through that terminal outcome, not merely through an intermediate panel open. Exercise keyboard and pointer routes together when they represent the same semantic action. Keep deliberate clear/reset commands as protected counterexamples so preservation rules do not make state impossible to clear intentionally.

4. BASELINE WHEN IT ADDS SIGNAL
When safe and affordable, exercise representative protected controls on the known-good reference in an isolated worktree/build/runtime and record the result. Then run the same controls on the candidate.
If baseline execution is impractical, use durable prior evidence and current contract tests, clearly marking the lower proof level. Never pretend a historical green badge is a fresh live baseline.

5. RUN AUTOMATED REGRESSIONS
Run in dependency-aware order:
- focused tests for the changed behavior;
- focused protected controls for impacted existing behavior;
- caller/integration tests across changed seams;
- migration/upgrade/retry/idempotency tests where the change affects persisted or transitional state;
- broader suite/build/static checks when practical.
Add a regression that reproduces every concrete regression found. Keep valid counterexamples. Do not modify expected results, snapshots, fixtures, mocks, or tolerances merely to fit the broken candidate unless the product contract truly changed and that change is explicitly supported by the request.

6. RUN THE CANONICAL LIVE PATH WHEN THE CLAIM IS LIVE
If the feature is an app/browser/service/CLI/device/operator workflow and a safe executable environment exists, do not stop at synthetic tests. Use the product's canonical launcher/entrypoint and exercise:
A. the requested new/repaired behavior; and
B. at least one impacted previously working control.
Observe the actual result, not only route issuance, command ACK, process exit, or mocked output. Collect bounded evidence/logs. If live proof requires inaccessible credentials, protected hardware/runtime, destructive action, or explicit operator authorization, state the exact gate and proof ceiling; do not claim the regression closed at the live level.

7. REPAIR WITHOUT TRADING ONE BUG FOR ANOTHER
When a protected behavior fails:
- locate the smallest canonical owner;
- preserve the requested new behavior and the old valid behavior together;
- repair implementation/contract migration rather than weakening the regression gate;
- rerun the failing control plus the new feature path immediately;
- inspect adjacent callers for the same break mechanism.
If the failure generalizes into a broader defect class, use the failure-class audit pattern; if tests bypass the real production boundary, use the production-path proof-gap pattern.

8. DELIBERATE SECOND PASS
After first green:
- inspect the diff, test changes, mocks/fixtures/snapshots, impacted call stacks, and live evidence again;
- ask `What behavior could this change break that our selected tests would not notice?`;
- add or run the smallest practical missing control;
- repeat repair/revalidation for concrete gaps.
Stop at a bounded fixed point; do not manufacture test volume.

9. AUTONOMY
Run the tests, worktrees, builds, launchers, fixtures, logs, and safe live checks yourself when tools permit. Do not make the user a regression runner or evidence courier. Escalate only a genuine inaccessible runtime/credential/physical/authorization gate.

DELIVER
Report: reference fixed point; candidate head; protected-behavior ledger; impact/call-stack map; automated regressions run; live controls run; regressions found/repaired; before/after evidence; tests added/changed; second-pass result; proof level/ceiling; remaining blocked controls; commit/PR/integration state.

ROUTING BOUNDARY
- Use failure-class auditing when one regression exposes a reusable defect class.
- Use production-path proof-gap auditing when tests and the actual execution path differ.
- Use the dedicated live-runtime executor for a deeper protected runtime proof sprint.
- Use closure certification only after preservation and requested behavior are both proved at the claimed level.

prompts.name: Program Design & Call-Stack Prototype Architect
prompts.sprintRole: Design the program between governance/harness and implementation by widening the solution space, defining domain seams, state/data ownership, interfaces, failure contracts, and executable call-stack prototypes for the highest-value user journeys
prompts.useWhen: A product or subsystem needs a coherent software design before broad implementation: doctrine and harness may exist, but module boundaries, call stacks, ownership, adapters, state transitions, error propagation, and test seams are not yet proven.
prompts.inspectFirst: User outcomes/use cases and terminology; current code and entrypoints; P00-style governance and P01-style harness if present; existing modules/interfaces/state models; dependency graph; persistence/external services; known failure modes; tests/prototypes; performance/security/concurrency constraints; current architecture decisions and rejected alternatives. For user-facing journeys, identify the terminal user value and current interaction count/state transitions so an intermediate screen or focus target is not mistaken for completion. When design uncertainty is material, inspect a bounded set of relevant external repositories or structurally analogous systems for implementation mechanisms before locking local seams. Do not infer whole-program architecture from one isolated file: acquire cohesive repository context covering the relevant tree, root manifests/configuration, entrypoints, state owners, composition/routing, tests, and dependency declarations before making repository-wide claims. If direct repository access is unavailable, use a bounded repo bundle or tree-plus-root-config fallback and state the resulting proof limit.
prompts.expectedOutput: A compact program design with precise domain vocabulary, module/interface/seam map, state/data ownership, dependency direction, representative success/failure call stacks, thin executable prototypes through the proposed seams, evidence-backed design decisions, and an implementation-ready proof ceiling without prematurely building the whole product. User-facing call stacks also identify the terminal value action, redundant intermediate states, and any product-usage telemetry owner needed for explicitly requested personalization. When useful, include materially different candidate concepts and the local adaptations required before prototype evidence selects one.
prompts.nextStep: Choose the highest-risk user journey; when design uncertainty is material, scan a bounded set of relevant external repositories or structurally analogous systems, synthesize 2-4 materially different candidate mechanisms, then prototype the strongest competing seams with real domain logic. Inspect success/error traces and converge only after evidence selects the design.
prompts.proofGate: The design is derived from user outcomes rather than folder aesthetics; important state/data has one owner; dependency direction and side-effect boundaries are explicit; core modules hide meaningful behavior behind small interfaces; representative call stacks execute through the proposed seams; failure/error propagation is prototyped; competing seam choices are compared when materially uncertain; and the result is testable and implementation-ready without pretending prototype proof is production proof. A representative user journey is not considered successful merely because an intermediate panel rendered: the prototype reaches the stated terminal user value with intentional state transitions and no unexplained redundant step. External inspiration must be tied to inspected source/tests/config and locally adapted; exhaustive ecosystem research remains P97's job. Repository-wide architecture claims are grounded in cohesive repository context, or are explicitly limited when only partial context is available.

prompts.name: Open-Source Prior-Art & Gap Analyst
prompts.sprintRole: Study relevant open-source implementations before local design so the team can distinguish already-solved real-world mechanics from the project-specific gap that still deserves development.
prompts.useWhen: A repository is about to design or build a meaningful capability and similar open-source systems may already exist, especially when the operator says to analyze repositories that have already done something like this so the local solution can emulate proven patterns rather than reinventing them.
prompts.inspectFirst: The requested capability and acceptance boundary; current repository implementation, contracts, tests, architecture, active PRs, and known gaps; then a bounded set of genuinely relevant open-source repositories with source, tests, configuration, releases, issues, documentation, commit/tag identity, and license evidence sufficient to verify the mechanisms being compared.
prompts.expectedOutput: A source-backed reference matrix, pattern disposition ledger, explicit solved-baseline-versus-local-gap map, and one prioritized bounded development target or executable handoff that names what to emulate, what to adapt, what to reject, what remains unknown, and why.
prompts.nextStep: Take the highest-value project-specific gap from the evidence-backed gap map and route it into the repository's canonical design/build owner, preserving the selected reference mechanism and proof criteria; if the current request already authorizes that implementation and the environment supports it, continue into that bounded owner instead of stopping at a research essay.
prompts.proofGate: Each claimed precedent is tied to a concrete repository and current enough source evidence; observed implementation is separated from documentation, inference, and absence; reusable mechanics are distinguished from code that should not be copied; the current repository is rechecked before declaring a gap; every candidate pattern is dispositioned; and the final prioritized gap is materially narrower and better evidenced than the original vague problem statement.

prompts.name: User-Flow Friction & Preference Telemetry Refiner
prompts.sprintRole: Repair technically-working but inefficient user journeys by preserving orthogonal state, collapsing redundant interaction steps, instrumenting semantic completion events, and deriving privacy-bounded preference views from real usage rather than guesswork
prompts.useWhen: A product feature technically works but the user journey loses unrelated state, requires redundant intermediate UI, makes shortcuts stop short of the user's real goal, or needs usage evidence to personalize navigation, favorites, recommendations, or an interactive most-used dashboard, or the default view buries primary content under persistent filter/control chrome before the user's material begins.
prompts.inspectFirst: The user's exact starting state and terminal goal; current interaction sequence and keyboard/pointer entrypoints; state owners for search/filter/focus/selection/detail panels; copy/toast or other completion feedback; existing telemetry/preferences/storage contracts; privacy/data-retention constraints; current interaction/regression/live tests and accepted behavior.
prompts.expectedOutput: A measured before/after flow with a journey-state ledger, redundant-step removals, explicit preservation rules for orthogonal UI state, direct terminal actions, semantic usage-event ownership, deterministic preference aggregation, a bounded interactive usage dashboard when requested, focused sequence regressions, and live-path proof at the strongest safe level.
prompts.nextStep: Replay the highest-friction user journey from its real entrypoint, write its state/action/terminal-outcome sequence, identify the first destructive or redundant transition, repair that canonical owner, instrument only the semantic completion event that represents real use, then rerun the journey plus one protected neighboring sequence before expanding the dashboard or personalization surface.
prompts.proofGate: The repaired journey reaches the user's terminal goal with fewer unnecessary steps; controls that do not semantically own search/filter/focus/selection state do not erase it; keyboard and pointer routes converge on the same semantic action; completion feedback reflects the actual completed action; usage counts increment exactly once per qualifying completion rather than panel-open/view events; preference data has an explicit storage/privacy/reset boundary; dashboard values are derived from persisted events rather than hard-coded ordering; and focused sequence tests plus the strongest practical live path pass without regressing existing navigation; default-view repairs reduce measured first-viewport consumption before primary content instead of only hiding controls behind a toggle; shared telemetry/preferences authority is reused or explicitly authorized rather than silently widened by a local flow repair.
prompts.copyContent:
REFINE THE USER FLOW, NOT JUST THE INDIVIDUAL CONTROL. FIX REDUNDANT INTERACTION STEPS, PRESERVE ORTHOGONAL STATE, AND USE SEMANTIC USAGE EVIDENCE WHEN PERSONALIZATION OR A MOST-USED DASHBOARD IS IN SCOPE.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Journey or friction: recover from the current conversation/runtime evidence
Primary terminal user goal: xyz_terminal_goal_or_resolve_from_evidence

MISSION
Take a user journey that technically works but feels wrong, destructive, redundant, or opaque and make the flow match the user's actual goal. Treat search text, filters, focus, selections, panels, clipboard actions, notifications, and preference data as composed state with explicit owners. Optimize the complete sequence rather than declaring each button or hotkey correct in isolation. When the user wants personalization, measure semantic completions and derive the preference surface from those events without turning every hover, view, or panel-open into fake intent.

1. REPLAY THE REAL JOURNEY
Start from the exact user entrypoint and reproduce the interaction in order. Record a compact journey-state ledger with: step, input, state before, semantic action, state after, visible feedback, and whether the step advanced the terminal goal. Include keyboard and pointer routes when both are supported. Do not replace the user's stated friction with a designer-invented journey.

2. DEFINE THE TERMINAL USER VALUE
Name what the user is actually trying to accomplish. Opening a panel, moving focus, or revealing detail is not automatically success when the real goal is to copy, execute, submit, compare, navigate, or otherwise use the underlying object. Mark intermediate UI as scaffolding, not closure. Prefer the shortest understandable route that preserves discoverability and safety.

3. PRESERVE ORTHOGONAL STATE
For every control identify which state it owns and which state it must leave alone. A visibility toggle should not clear an active search unless clearing search is part of its documented semantic contract. A panel open/close action should not destroy unrelated selections, filters, or query state. Make destructive transitions explicit. Add sequence regressions that combine controls, because isolated-key tests cannot prove composed state.

4. COLLAPSE REDUNDANT INTERMEDIATE STEPS
Find steps that merely expose a control for an action the initiating shortcut already unambiguously means to perform. If a favorite-item shortcut semantically means 'use this favorite' and the safe terminal action is copy, invoke the canonical copy action directly, reuse the normal success toast/feedback, and keep existing panel/navigation commands available separately. Do not create duplicate close/clear rituals when another supported command already owns them. Preserve accessibility and an obvious way to inspect detail when inspection is genuinely requested.

5. REPAIR THE DEFAULT INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE
Measure how much of the initial viewport is consumed before primary content as a flow-economy metric. Persistent control density is friction even when every control works. Prefer classification -> progressive disclosure -> subordinate choices; parents first, then only in-scope subcategories. A Hide/Show toggle reduces clutter on demand but does not fix a noisy default information architecture. Reuse deterministic existing classifications; preserve search, keyboard and mobile use, Favorites, and active-state semantics.

6. UNIFY ENTRYPOINTS ON SEMANTIC ACTIONS
Keyboard shortcuts, buttons, command palette items, touch controls, and automation should call the same domain-level action where they mean the same thing. Do not let one path mutate search/filter/detail state differently just because it was implemented by another listener. Keep state ownership, feedback, and error behavior centralized.

7. INSTRUMENT SEMANTIC USAGE, NOT NOISE
When personalization or usage analytics is requested, define the smallest event contract that represents meaningful completion. Examples: prompt copied, prompt executed, artifact exported, workflow completed. Do not count focus, hover, panel-open, detail-view, or failed attempts as successful use unless the product explicitly needs a separate diagnostic metric. Make increment semantics idempotent enough that one user action cannot double-count through bubbling or duplicate handlers.

8. OWN PREFERENCE DATA EXPLICITLY
Define event identity, item ID, timestamp or bucket only when needed, storage owner, schema/version, retention/reset behavior, device/profile/account scope, migration, and failure behavior. Before mutating a shared telemetry/preferences owner, confirm this journey is authorized to own that schema or contract change; otherwise reuse the existing owner and route the shared-owner change separately instead of expanding scope implicitly. Prefer local/private storage for local-only personalization unless the product already owns authenticated sync. Never collect prompt bodies, secrets, clipboard contents, or other sensitive payloads merely to count usage. Provide a clear reset/export path when that matches existing portability patterns.

9. DERIVE THE DASHBOARD FROM EVENTS
If an interactive most-used/preferences dashboard is in scope, derive it from the canonical aggregated event store. Show useful dimensions only: usage count, recent use, favorite status, category/type, or trend when supported by actual data. Let users filter/sort/drill into the same canonical prompt/item identities. Do not hard-code rank order or maintain a second preference truth. Empty/new-user state must be useful and honest.

10. TEST SEQUENCES AND FAILURE STATES
Add focused tests for the actual compositions that failed or could fail:
- active search -> unrelated filter show/hide/toggle -> query and matching results preserved;
- favorite shortcut -> terminal action occurs once -> normal success feedback appears -> no unnecessary detail panel required;
- pointer and keyboard versions of the same semantic action produce equivalent state and telemetry;
- storage failure does not fake a successful preference write;
- duplicate event dispatch does not double-count one completion;
- reset/migration preserves the documented boundary;
- dashboard derives from stored usage and updates after a qualifying action.
Protect existing deliberate clear/reset/navigation behaviors as controls.

11. MEASURE FLOW ECONOMY
Compare before/after using concrete interaction evidence: steps/keystrokes, focus changes, unnecessary panel transitions, destructive state resets, time-to-terminal-action where practical, and qualitative operator friction already supplied. Do not optimize for fewer clicks when the removed step carried necessary safety, confirmation, or comprehension.

12. LIVE-PATH PROOF
Run the canonical browser/app path when safely available. Reproduce the original friction, execute the repaired sequence, observe actual clipboard/notification/state/dashboard behavior, and run at least one protected neighboring path. Static tests prove contracts; they do not prove browser focus, clipboard permissions, event ordering, or rendered-dashboard behavior. State the exact proof ceiling when the live path is inaccessible.

DELIVER
Report the original journey, terminal goal, destructive/redundant steps, state-owner changes, semantic event contract, privacy/storage boundary, dashboard derivation, before/after flow evidence, focused sequence tests, live proof, commit/PR/merge state, and any remaining product-only decision.

ROUTING BOUNDARY
Use the generic Prototype-Measure-Refine loop when the main problem is broad experimentation rather than user-flow friction. Use Program Design & Call-Stack Prototype Architect when module/state ownership itself is still unresolved. Use Regression Test & Live Behavior Guard to protect already accepted behaviors around the change. This prompt owns the product-flow repair plus preference-telemetry/dashboard slice when those concerns are coupled by the user journey.

prompts.name: Permissioned Repository Polling & Scheduled Sync Builder
prompts.sprintRole: Analyze a repository, then implement a user-controlled local polling loop that detects authoritative upstream changes and performs only the repository-approved bounded synchronization needed to keep a consumer current
prompts.useWhen: A repository or local application should periodically check another repository, artifact, service, or version source for newer authoritative state and optionally synchronize it on a user-controlled schedule, rather than relying on a human or agent to remember repeated manual checks.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current repository governance and default-branch truth; existing updater/acquisition/launcher surfaces; authoritative upstream identity and version/change signal; consumer ownership boundary; user/profile configuration conventions; scheduler/service integration already present; local repository/worktree state; cache/download/output roots; validators/tests; secrets/network boundaries; logs/receipts; and any existing retry, lock, backoff, or single-instance mechanism.
prompts.expectedOutput: A repository-native polling capability with an explicit enable/disable control, configurable cadence, cheap authoritative change probe, idempotent no-change path, safe update action, profile-aware local state, single-instance/concurrency protection, bounded failure/backoff behavior, durable last-seen/last-applied receipt, scheduler integration appropriate to the host, focused tests, and live proof at the strongest safe level without silently enabling recurring local-machine mutation.
prompts.nextStep: Run one foreground poll against the exact configured upstream, prove both no-change and newer-version decision paths with repository-safe fixtures or a controlled upstream identity, then register or enable the real schedule only when the current user-controlled toggle or explicit authorization allows that local-machine mutation.
prompts.proofGate: The poller analyzes and reuses repository ownership before adding machinery; the authoritative change signal is explicit; disabled means no scheduled mutation; no-change performs no payload rewrite; one upstream identity is applied at most once; dirty/divergent/local-only work is preserved rather than reset; overlapping runs cannot race; failures back off without inventing success; state/cache paths are bounded and profile-aware; the user can inspect and disable the schedule; receipts distinguish observed, applied, skipped, blocked, and failed runs; and focused plus live/scheduler proof reaches only the level actually observed.
prompts.copyContent:
BUILD A PERMISSIONED POLLING LOOP AFTER ANALYZING THE REPOSITORY. IMPLEMENT THE REAL SCHEDULED SYNC CAPABILITY; DO NOT STOP AT A TIMER, CRON EXAMPLE, OR DESIGN NOTE.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Polling target / authoritative upstream: xyz_upstream_or_resolve_from_repository_evidence
Desired local profile or runtime: xyz_profile_or_resolve_from_current_environment
Cadence: xyz_interval_or_resolve_from_existing_product/config requirements

MISSION
Analyze the repository first, then add the smallest durable polling capability that periodically checks an authoritative upstream identity and performs the repository-approved update only when newer state exists. The capability must be user-controlled, safely repeatable, observable, and easy for both users and agents to rely on. Treat polling as a state machine around an existing ownership/update path, not as permission to create a second source of truth or blindly pull on a timer.

1. ANALYZE THE REPOSITORY BEFORE DESIGNING THE POLLER
Read current governance, codebase/harness maps, updater/acquisition/launcher commands, config/profile ownership, artifact/version registries, scheduler/service hooks, tests, validators, logs/receipts, and recent failures. Identify the canonical consumer, canonical upstream, current manual update path, and which existing function should own the actual synchronization. Reuse that path instead of implementing a parallel downloader or repository mutator.

2. DEFINE AUTHORITY AND THE CHANGE SIGNAL
Choose one explicit authoritative identity that answers `is there anything new?`: Git commit SHA/ref, release/version, manifest hash, ETag, artifact digest, schema/version pair, API revision, or the repository's existing equivalent. Prefer a cheap metadata/identity probe before downloading or rebuilding payloads. Mirrors, cached copies, Drive/OneDrive distributions, or locally generated artifacts do not outrank the canonical upstream merely because they are easier to read. Persist the last observed and last successfully applied identity separately when that distinction matters.

3. USER CONSENT AND ENABLE/DISABLE OWNERSHIP
Recurring local execution is opt-in product state. Reuse an existing settings/profile owner when one exists; otherwise add the smallest explicit enabled/disabled setting plus cadence/config needed by the repository. Default new recurring mutation to disabled unless current repository policy or an already-approved user setting explicitly says otherwise. The user must be able to inspect whether polling is enabled, see the configured target/cadence, trigger one foreground check, and disable/unregister the schedule without deleting unrelated configuration. Do not hide scheduler installation behind an ordinary app launch or import.

4. IMPLEMENT A SMALL POLL STATE MACHINE
Make the decisions explicit and testable: DISABLED -> PROBE -> NO_CHANGE | UPDATE_AVAILABLE -> APPLY -> VALIDATE -> APPLIED, with BLOCKED/FAILED paths where needed. NO_CHANGE IS A SUCCESSFUL TERMINAL STATE and must not rewrite payloads, touch unrelated files, create commits, or duplicate cached artifacts. Record enough durable state to explain the last decision after restart without turning the state file into a second implementation database.

5. MAKE THE UPDATE ACTION SAFE AND IDEMPOTENT
Call the repository's canonical acquisition/update function after the probe says an update is needed. For Git-backed consumers, preserve dirty work, local-only commits, divergence, and separately owned work; use fetch/compare plus fast-forward-only or an isolated clean worktree according to repository policy. Never reset, clean, force-pull, or overwrite unique work just because a scheduled run wants freshness. For artifact consumers, validate expected schema/version/digest before replacing the active copy and use atomic staging/rename or the repository's equivalent so an interrupted update cannot leave a half-written active artifact. Applying the same upstream identity twice must be a no-op.

6. KEEP LOCAL STATE PROFILE-AWARE AND BOUNDED
Use one stable repository-approved or user/profile-scoped root for poll state, locks, cache, and receipts. Derive the actual platform/user/profile path from existing harness/configuration instead of hard-coding usernames, Desktop layouts, OneDrive locations, or a developer's machine. Do not create a fresh clone, cache tree, temp directory, or generated-site copy every interval. Define bounded retention/cleanup for disposable downloads and stale receipts while preserving the current active artifact and evidence needed for recovery. Distinct local profiles must not silently share mutable poll state unless the product explicitly owns shared state.

7. INTEGRATE WITH THE HOST SCHEDULER, NOT AN ACCIDENTAL FOREVER LOOP
Prefer the repository/platform's normal scheduler boundary: Windows Task Scheduler, cron, systemd timer, launchd, an existing service/daemon, or an application-owned scheduler when that is already canonical. Keep the poll operation itself foreground-runnable and independently testable; the scheduler should invoke it, not contain the business logic. Use a configurable conservative cadence instead of inventing an aggressive interval. Avoid busy waits. Add jitter only when fleet-wide synchronization or thundering-herd evidence makes it useful. Preserve exit codes so the scheduler can distinguish success, blocked state, and failure.

8. PROTECT AGAINST OVERLAP, OFFLINE STATE, AND FAILURE STORMS
Use a single-instance lock, compare-and-set, scheduler policy, or another repository-appropriate guard so two due runs cannot apply the same update concurrently. Bound network/tool timeouts and retries. Back off after repeated transient failures; classify permanent/auth/configuration failures separately. Do not retry unsafe mutations blindly. Offline or unreachable upstream must leave the last known-good consumer intact and produce an actionable receipt rather than pretending the local copy is current.

9. MAKE EACH RUN OBSERVABLE WITHOUT CREATING LOG BLOAT
Record a compact receipt or structured status with timestamp, configured upstream, observed identity, prior applied identity, decision (`disabled`, `no-change`, `update-available`, `applied`, `blocked`, `failed`), validation result, and failure class when applicable. Do not log secrets, prompt bodies, clipboard contents, credentials, or protected payloads merely to prove a check happened. Bound retention according to existing repository logging/state patterns. Expose a simple status command or UI surface when the product already has one.

10. TEST THE DECISIONS, NOT JUST THE TIMER
Add focused deterministic cases for: disabled; first run; no change; newer identity; repeated same identity; malformed/unknown manifest or schema; dirty/divergent Git state; interrupted staging; overlapping runs; offline/timeout; failed validation; scheduler command construction; profile-specific state roots; disable/unregister; and restart/resume from the last receipt. Prove the real update function is invoked only on the intended transition. A unit test that merely calls a callback every N seconds is not polling proof.

11. RUN LIVE AND SCHEDULED PROOF AT THE STRONGEST SAFE LEVEL
Run one foreground poll through the canonical entrypoint. Exercise or simulate both no-change and update-available paths without corrupting authoritative state. When local-machine authorization is already present, register/enable the schedule and verify the scheduler points at the canonical executable/config and can execute one bounded run. When authorization is not present, leave the schedule disabled and prove the exact enable path rather than silently crossing the user-only gate. Report whether actual due-time execution was observed or only scheduler registration/configuration was proven.

12. AGENTSWITCHBOARD / PROMPT KIT REFERENCE USE CASE
A valid application is an AgentSwitchboard profile that periodically checks `EndeavorEverlasting/web-excel-repair-triage` for a newer Prompt Kit identity and refreshes the local consumable only after the user enables polling. Keep GitHub/the canonical Triage repository authoritative. AgentSwitchboard should consume the Prompt Kit through its existing launcher/profile or bounded adapter rather than owning a duplicate prompt registry or rewriting prompt IDs. Prefer the established safe acquisition semantics: discover the real user/profile path, clone only when absent, otherwise fetch and compare current upstream, fast-forward only when safe, refuse destructive repair of dirty/divergent work, validate the acquired Prompt Kit before activation, and keep the active local path stable so users and agents can iterate without directory bloat. Treat this as an example, not a requirement that every poller use Git.

DELIVER
Report: repository analysis and existing owner reused; authoritative upstream/change identity; enable/disable and cadence ownership; poll state machine; local/profile state paths; scheduler integration; update safety/idempotency; lock/backoff behavior; status/receipt surface; focused tests; foreground/live/scheduled proof; files changed; commit/PR/merge state; proof ceiling; and the exact next executable action. Do not claim the poller is operational merely because a scheduled-task definition or timer exists.

prompts.name: Prompt Registry Classification Refiner
prompts.sprintRole: Iteratively review the full Prompt Kit classification model, prototype bounded taxonomy improvements, turn discovered invariants into executable hooks, and converge the validated classification system to main without renaming canonical prompt identities merely to fit the taxonomy
prompts.useWhen: Prompt Kit classes, types, profiles, categories, colors, keywords, filters, or discovery behavior have drifted, overlap confusingly, classify similar prompts inconsistently, or need a deliberate registry-wide classification pass that improves the taxonomy and its enforcement rather than hand-editing a few labels.
prompts.inspectFirst: Current default-branch Prompt Kit registries and generated site; classification fields and their actual consumers; filter/search/discovery behavior; prompt IDs/titles as stable identity; adjacent alias/synonym or intent-routing mechanisms so presentation aliases and discovery synonyms are not mistaken for taxonomy; existing classification tests, builders, validators, hooks, CI, and recent overlapping prompt/filter work.
prompts.expectedOutput: A measured classification baseline, explicit field semantics and ownership, one or more bounded prototype migrations, executable hooks or validators for every newly proven invariant that can be checked deterministically, focused regression coverage, generated-site parity, preserved canonical prompt identities, and the exact validated classification result integrated into current main.
prompts.nextStep: Classify the current registry baseline, choose the smallest high-value ambiguity as prototype 1, implement that classification slice plus its enforceable hook, rebuild and falsify it through the real Prompt Kit filters/search, then continue from the new evidence until no bounded classification defect remains and merge the exact green head to main.
prompts.proofGate: Every classification field has a non-overlapping documented role grounded in current consumers; canonical prompt IDs and useful titles survive reclassification; aliases, human display titles, keywords, and intent/discovery synonyms are not silently promoted into canonical taxonomy; each iteration is an executable prototype with before/after evidence; every deterministic invariant discovered during the sprint is enforced by the nearest practical validator/hook before the next migration slice; generated registry/site parity and focused classification behavior pass on the exact head; and the validated result is contained in refreshed main.
prompts.copyContent:
REFINE THE PROMPT KIT CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM ITERATIVELY. REVIEW THE WHOLE REGISTRY, IMPLEMENT HOOKS AS CLASSIFICATION RULES BECOME PROVABLE, AND CONVERGE THE EXACT VALIDATED RESULT TO MAIN. DO NOT RENAME PROMPTS MERELY TO MAKE THE TAXONOMY LOOK CLEAN.

Repo: `EndeavorEverlasting/web-excel-repair-triage` or resolve the current Prompt Kit repository from context
Classification pain, if known: xyz_classification_gap_or_infer_from_evidence

MISSION
Treat Prompt Kit classification as an engineered information architecture, not a one-time relabeling exercise. Inspect the full effective registry and the UI/discovery surfaces that consume it; make the smallest useful classification improvement; run it as a real prototype; falsify the result; convert each proven classification invariant into an executable hook or validator as you go; then repeat until the bounded classification system reaches a fixed point and the exact green result is integrated into current main.

1. REFRESH AND BASELINE THE ACTUAL CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM
Start from refreshed default-branch truth. Inspect the combined registry, generated Prompt Kit, builder, filter/search/discovery consumers, registry helper, focused tests, hooks/CI, and overlapping prompt/filter branches or PRs. Inventory the fields that currently participate in identity, classification, presentation, and discovery. Do not infer semantics from field names alone.

Build a compact baseline that answers for every relevant field: what it means today, who writes it, who consumes it, allowed/current values, collisions/near-duplicates, empty or overloaded buckets, and whether it is identity, taxonomy, presentation, or discovery metadata. Measure practical defects such as ambiguous labels, inconsistent sibling prompts, filter branches that mean different things in different places, singletons that should be merged, overloaded classes that need a useful split, or discovery keywords doing work that belongs in taxonomy.

2. KEEP IDENTITY, TAXONOMY, PRESENTATION, AND DISCOVERY DISTINCT
Preserve canonical prompt IDs and useful prompt names unless a separate explicit rename requirement exists. Classification work must not manufacture new prompt identities merely because a different label sounds better.

Determine the repository-specific meaning of fields such as `type`, `class`, `profile`, `category`, `color`, and `keywords` from current code and contracts before changing them. In particular:
- stable ID/name are identity, not a classification migration target by default;
- human aliases/display titles are presentation identity, not canonical taxonomy;
- keywords, triggers, and intent synonyms primarily serve discovery/routing unless the repository explicitly assigns them another role;
- color is visual semantics unless current consumers prove it is a classification axis;
- profile/registry placement is ownership or behavior only to the extent current builders/tests actually use it.
Do not collapse these systems into one universal label.

3. ITERATE AS PROTOTYPES, NOT AS A BIG-BANG TAXONOMY REWRITE
Use this loop:
`BASELINE -> HYPOTHESIS -> SMALLEST PROTOTYPE -> REBUILD -> USE/FALSIFY -> HOOK -> MIGRATE NEXT SLICE -> REFRESH -> CONTINUE`.

Prototype 1 should attack the highest-value bounded ambiguity, not attempt to rename the whole registry. Exercise the prototype through the real Prompt Kit UI/filter/search/discovery path or the closest executable consumer. Compare before/after behavior and inspect surprising prompts at both sides of the boundary. A prototype is evidence; it is not automatically the final taxonomy.

After each pass, ask what the result taught you about the classification model. Keep the successful invariant, repair the failed hypothesis, or revert the slice if evidence says the old boundary was better. Continue with the next smallest migration only after the prior classification rule is understandable and protected.

4. IMPLEMENT HOOKS AS YOU LEARN THE RULES
Whenever an iteration establishes a deterministic invariant, enforce it immediately in the nearest existing owner rather than leaving the rule as prose. Reuse current validation/harness patterns. Examples include registry validation, focused semantic assertions, allowed-value checks, uniqueness or normalization checks, classification-consumer parity, generated-site checks, pre-commit/pre-push hooks, or CI path triggers.

Do not add a hook for subjective judgment that cannot be checked reliably. Do not create one giant universal classifier merely to centralize everything. Prefer small checks at the boundary that owns the invariant. A later prototype may strengthen an earlier hook when new evidence reveals an edge case.

5. CLASSIFY BY BEHAVIOR AND CLOSURE, NOT TITLE ALONE
When deciding where a prompt belongs, compare trigger, mission, owned scope, expected output, proof gate, and closure condition. Similar wording does not imply the same class; different wording does not imply different classes. Use representative sibling prompts and boundary cases to test each proposed class.

If the taxonomy needs a new value, prove that existing values cannot express the distinction without making discovery/filtering worse. If two values mean the same thing in practice, migrate toward one canonical value and protect it. Preserve intentional distinctions where downstream behavior or user navigation benefits from them.

6. PROVE DISCOVERY AND FILTER BEHAVIOR
Rebuild the canonical Prompt Kit after each tracked classification migration. Exercise hierarchical filters, search, prompt identifiers, favorites/hotkeys when classification metadata participates, and any registry/profile views affected by the change. Confirm that a user can still find the expected prompts by natural language and canonical ID. Classification cleanup must not silently break search/discovery or turn synonyms into taxonomy.

7. SECOND-PASS FALSIFICATION
After the first apparently green classification state, inspect the registry from the opposite direction: sample prompts from every changed bucket, inspect neighboring unchanged buckets, search for old/new classification labels, run edge-case filter combinations, and review generated output plus focused tests. Turn every concrete in-scope miss into another prototype pass. Do not manufacture churn when the evidence reaches a bounded fixed point.

8. CONVERGE TO MAIN
Refresh the remote default branch immediately before final proof. Reconcile moved base/dependencies without discarding owned work. Run the strongest focused classification tests, registry helper validation, generated-site parity/build checks, filter/search/discovery regressions, applicable hook/CI checks, and `git diff --check`. If the exact validated head is merge-authorized and clean, merge it into current main in the same sprint. After merge, refresh main and prove containment of the integrated SHA rather than requiring head equality if main advanced again.

DELIVER
Report: baseline classification defects; field-semantics map; each prototype hypothesis and result; classification migrations; hooks/validators added or strengthened; prompts intentionally left unchanged and why; generated-site/filter/discovery proof; commit/PR/merge state; resulting main SHA; remaining classification debt or `none` at the bounded fixed point.

FAIL-CLOSED
Do not perform a registry-wide relabeling without an executable prototype and rollback boundary. Do not rename stable IDs/titles as a substitute for classification. Do not confuse aliases or human-facing artifact names with taxonomy. Do not treat search keywords/intent synonyms as canonical class labels merely because they improve discovery. Do not weaken hooks/tests to accept the migration. Do not stop at a green feature branch while safe authorized mainline integration remains.

MISSION
Add or strengthen a tracked mechanism by which the repository can deterministically generate bounded code updates from canonical inputs in addition to changes authored by human or agent developers. The repository-owned mechanism must have a smaller authority surface than a general coding agent: explicit inputs, a canonical generator entrypoint, declared output ownership, fail-closed boundaries, validation, provenance, and ordinary Git integration. Implement the mechanism and prove the real call path; do not stop at a workflow sketch.

1. RECOVER EXISTING GENERATION AUTHORITY
Refresh remote/default-branch truth first. Inspect existing builders, generators, schemas, registries, manifests, workflows, hooks, generated-file banners, tests, and operator docs. Build canonical input -> generator -> generated surface -> trigger -> validator -> integration gate. Reuse a compatible owner instead of creating a second codegen system. An ad-hoc provider replay script is transport, not automatically the canonical generator.

2. DRAW THE SOURCE / GENERATED BOUNDARY
Define authoritative inputs/schema/version, one canonical generator, exact owned output paths, forbidden paths/data classes, committed-vs-ephemeral status, provenance, and the validator/build/test for every generated surface. Generated output must not become competing truth. Humans and agents repair canonical input/template/generator and regenerate unless policy explicitly names another owner.

3. MAKE GENERATION DETERMINISTIC AND IDEMPOTENT
Same accepted inputs plus pinned generator/dependency versions must produce semantically identical output. Normalize unstable ordering, timestamps, machine-local paths, random identifiers, locale, and environment leakage unless intentional. First execution may create a bounded diff; an immediate unchanged-input repeat must produce zero tracked diff.

4. FAIL CLOSED AT THE MUTATION BOUNDARY
Validate inputs and destinations before destructive writes. Prefer staging plus atomic replacement, transaction-like commit, or rollback to last-known-good over partial mutation. Reject path traversal, symlink escape where relevant, undeclared outputs, malformed/partial inputs, missing dependencies, and secrets/private evidence entering public generated surfaces. Report what changed on failure. Never force-reset/push or erase separately owned work for convenience.

5. COEXIST WITH AGENT AND HUMAN DEVELOPERS
Enforce one writer per generated surface. Refresh/reconcile if another lane changed canonical input or generated output since the generation floor. On conflict, reconcile at the canonical source boundary; never let generated output silently overwrite separately owned work.

6. CHOOSE TRIGGERS WITHOUT CREATING A RECURSIVE BOT
Expose the smallest real repo CLI/script first; provider workflows delegate to it instead of duplicating logic. Add only justified triggers and loop guards so generated commits cannot cause an infinite generate-commit-generate cycle.

7. KEEP GENERATED CHANGES REVIEWABLE
Generated code is proposed code, not privileged truth. Produce a reviewable diff and generation receipt with input identity, generator identity, outputs, validation result, and proof ceiling. Respect branch protection/review/integration gates.

8. PROTOTYPE THE REAL CALL STACK
Exercise canonical input -> validation -> generator -> staged output -> owned-path guard -> write -> validator/test -> Git diff/receipt. Exercise malformed input, out-of-scope destination, stale/conflicting state, and failed/interrupted generation where practical.

9. PROVE REPEATABILITY AND INTEGRATION
Prove expected first-run diff, focused tests/validators, zero-diff repeat, rejection of undeclared output, provenance, same-entrypoint provider execution when claimed, and default-branch containment. Separate static/schema, unit/helper, same-entrypoint synthetic, provider runtime, and user/production proof.

10. STOP AT A BOUNDED FIXED POINT
Inspect diff, repeat behavior, failure receipts, trigger behavior, collision policy, artifacts, and CI evidence again. Repair concrete gaps. Stop when the declared surface is reproducible and no practical corruption, recursion, stale-state, or competing-writer gap remains.

DELIVER
Report ownership map; generator/trigger; inputs; owned/forbidden outputs; first/repeat diff; failure/collision/loop proof; validators; receipt/provenance; commit/integration; proof ceiling; exact next generator command or blocker. A workflow file or one bot commit alone is not completion.

prompts.name: Validated CI/CD Promotion Pipeline Builder
prompts.sprintRole: Design and implement a repository-owned GitHub Actions/CI/CD promotion mechanism that validates the exact candidate head through canonical harness and end-to-end test gates before automated push, merge, release, or deployment
prompts.useWhen: A repository should automatically validate code authored by humans, agents, or repo-native generators and then safely push, merge, release, or deploy that exact code through GitHub Actions/CI/CD rather than relying on manual promotion steps.
prompts.inspectFirst: Fresh default-branch/PR/workflow truth; current GitHub Actions and CI/CD files; branch protection, merge queue, environment/review rules and token permissions; canonical test/build/harness commands including P11-style harness validation; application E2E suites; artifact/package provenance; deployment/release paths; existing bot writers, concurrency groups, caches, retries, and prior pipeline failures.
prompts.expectedOutput: A tracked promotion architecture and implemented pipeline that delegates to repo-owned validation commands, pins proof to one exact candidate SHA, runs required harness validation and application E2E gates distinctly, preserves artifact provenance, fails closed on stale/moved/skipped/failed proof, serializes write authority, uses least privilege and loop guards, and performs only repository-authorized push/merge/release/deploy actions with provider-runtime evidence.
prompts.nextStep: Implement the smallest canary promotion path for one non-production candidate, trigger the real GitHub Actions workflow, prove one successful exact-head promotion and representative blocking failures, then broaden destinations only after those gates are stable. When a promotion gate fails with an agent-capable repair, emit the exact repair packet to P115 AFK Feedback-Driven Development Loop Executor; keep promotion blocked until a newly authored exact candidate returns through all required gates.
prompts.proofGate: The actual provider workflow validates one pinned candidate SHA through required static/unit/integration gates, the canonical harness validator, and applicable application E2E tests; required SKIP/FAIL/stale-head/moved-base/unauthorized-destination cases block promotion; artifacts are traceable to that SHA; concurrent/recursive writers are guarded; least-privilege permissions are explicit; and post-promotion default-branch/release/deployment evidence contains the proven candidate without bypassing repository protection.
prompts.copyContent:
DESIGN AND IMPLEMENT A VALIDATED REPOSITORY PROMOTION PIPELINE. USE GITHUB ACTIONS / CI-CD TO PUSH OR PROMOTE CODE ONLY AFTER THE EXACT CANDIDATE PASSES ITS REQUIRED HARNESS AND END-TO-END GATES. DO NOT CONFUSE PIPELINE AUTOMATION WITH CODE GENERATION OR BYPASS REPOSITORY PROTECTION.

Repo/product: xyz_repo_or_product
Promotion destination(s): xyz_branch_merge_release_deploy_targets
Existing CI/harness entrypoints, if known: xyz_commands_or_workflows
Required E2E surface, if known: xyz_cli_browser_service_device_or_other
Forbidden scope: xyz_forbidden_destinations_or_actions

MCP / SEMANTIC REPOSITORY RETRIEVAL CONTRACT
- FIRST EVIDENCE ACTION: when Augment Context Engine MCP is configured in the active Cursor environment, call its repository-retrieval tool before forming a repository-sensitive implementation plan or making repository-sensitive conclusions. Resolve the active MCP server/tool identity from Cursor; do not invent a tool name.
- Use separate bounded MCP retrievals for promotion authority, validation owners, proof/provenance, and write authority. Return the exact paths/owners found. Do not satisfy this contract with one vague or ceremonial MCP call, generic model knowledge, or ordinary local search alone.
- Then verify every material MCP finding against the actual checkout, refreshed Git state, GitHub/provider state, and repository-owned validators. MCP maps architecture; it does not prove current SHA/base, branch protection, PR/check status, credentials, deployment state, or promotion authority.
- If Augment MCP is unavailable, disconnected, unauthorized, or insufficient, report MCP_RETRIEVAL_BLOCKED and the resulting proof ceiling. Do not claim MCP-backed discovery or silently substitute assumptions.

MISSION
Build or strengthen the repository-owned mechanism that takes code already authored by humans, agent developers, or bounded repo-native generators and safely advances that exact revision through GitHub Actions/CI/CD validation to an authorized push, merge, release, or deployment. The pipeline is an evidence-and-promotion system, not another source-code author. It must compose canonical repo commands rather than duplicate them in YAML, distinguish harness end-to-end validation from application end-to-end testing, pin proof to an exact candidate identity, fail closed when proof is stale or incomplete, and produce provider-runtime evidence for the real promotion path.

1. RECOVER CURRENT PROMOTION AUTHORITY
Refresh all remote refs/tags and resolve the actual default branch. Inspect open/recent overlapping PRs/workflows, GitHub Actions, scripts/task runners, branch protection, merge queue, environments, required reviewers/checks, release/deploy machinery, bot identities, tokens/permissions, caches, artifacts, and current harness/test owners. Build event -> candidate SHA/base -> validation jobs -> artifacts -> approval/protection gates -> mutation/promotion action -> post-promotion proof. Reuse a compatible pipeline; do not create a second integration authority merely because another YAML file is easy.

2. SEPARATE AUTHORING, VALIDATION, AND PROMOTION
Code generation/authoring ends before promotion begins. A repo-native generator may propose a diff and humans/agents may author code, but this pipeline owns only validation and authorized advancement of the candidate. Preserve generated-surface ownership and one-writer rules. Never let CI rewrite source opportunistically unless a separately owned canonical generator explicitly requires that step.

3. BUILD THE VALIDATION DAG FROM CANONICAL COMMANDS
Define the cheapest-to-strongest graph appropriate to the repo: structural/schema/format -> lint/type/static -> unit -> integration -> build/package -> canonical harness E2E validator -> application/product E2E -> release/deploy-specific checks -> promotion. Do not require categories the product does not have, but every required existing gate needs one owner, command, inputs, outputs, and blocking semantics. GitHub Actions invokes repo-owned commands; YAML orchestrates and does not become a second test implementation.

4. KEEP HARNESS E2E AND APPLICATION E2E DISTINCT
Harness E2E validates repository contracts, validators, registries, fixtures, workflows, and proof machinery together. Application E2E validates user/system behavior through the real product entrypoint: CLI, browser, API/service, packaged binary, device/runtime, or another owned interface. Synthetic/offline harness PASS cannot substitute for live/application E2E, and an application smoke test cannot substitute for harness integrity. Compose both when required and report each proof level separately.

5. PIN EVERY GATE TO ONE CANDIDATE IDENTITY
Capture candidate head SHA, required base/merge-base, dependency/lock identities, and artifact identity before promotion. Every required job/receipt must be attributable to that candidate. If head, base, owning validator, required workflow, generated input, or artifact moves materially after proof, invalidate and rerun affected gates. Never promote whatever is currently on the branch after validating an earlier SHA. For merge queues/synthetic merge refs, record source head plus tested merge candidate.

6. DESIGN GITHUB ACTIONS TRIGGERS AND DEPENDENCIES EXPLICITLY
Use only justified events: pull_request for candidate validation, merge_group when merge queue is used, push for post-integration/release work, workflow_dispatch for bounded operator initiation, schedule/external events only when needed. Encode job dependencies so promotion cannot start before all required gates succeed. Path filters are optimization, not permission to skip a gate whose inputs changed indirectly. Prefer reusable workflows/actions when they remove duplicated orchestration without creating a second implementation.

7. FAIL CLOSED ON SKIP, STALE PROOF, AND PARTIAL SUCCESS
Classify gates REQUIRED / OPTIONAL / INAPPLICABLE / ENVIRONMENT-BLOCKED. REQUIRED plus SKIP is not green. Cancelled, timed-out, neutral, stale, or missing required results cannot satisfy promotion. `continue-on-error` is forbidden for promotion-critical gates unless downstream explicitly consumes and rejects the failure. Bounded retries may address identified transient infrastructure failures; deterministic test failures do not become green by repetition.

8. CONTROL WRITE AUTHORITY, CONCURRENCY, AND RECURSION
Use least-privilege GitHub token/action permissions and environment-scoped credentials. Separate read/validate jobs from write/promote jobs. Serialize mutation with concurrency or merge queue so two successful runs cannot race a branch/tag/deployment. Add actor/event/path/provenance guards so a bot promotion commit cannot recursively trigger another writer forever. Reject unauthorized destinations even if the token can technically write. Never echo secrets into logs/artifacts.

9. MAKE ARTIFACTS AND CACHES PART OF THE PROOF CHAIN
Prefer build-once/promote-the-same-artifact for deployable artifacts. Record source SHA, dependency/lock identity, build/run identity, checksums or equivalent immutable artifact identity, and destination. Cache hits may speed work but may not masquerade as fresh validation; keys/restoration rules must prevent stale artifacts or test outputs from satisfying a new candidate. Validate reused artifacts where trust boundaries require it.

10. DESIGN TEST ENVIRONMENT LIFECYCLE
For application E2E, define fixture/test-data creation, service/container/browser/runtime startup, readiness checks, isolated namespaces/accounts where applicable, bounded waits/retries, teardown, and cleanup. E2E tests must be repeatable and must not corrupt production/user state. When production-like infrastructure is unavailable, preserve the exact proof ceiling rather than silently downgrading the gate.

11. PROTOTYPE SUCCESS AND BLOCKING PATHS
Exercise the real provider workflow on the smallest safe canary candidate. Prove: green exact-head path reaches the authorized promotion action; harness-validator failure blocks it; application-E2E failure blocks it when required; required SKIP blocks; stale/moved candidate blocks; unauthorized target blocks; concurrent writer/merge-queue behavior is safe; recursion guard prevents a bot loop. Prefer targeted fault injection/fixtures over damaging real branches/environments.

11A. FAILED PROMOTION GATES FEED DEVELOPMENT; THEY DO NOT AUTHOR CODE HERE
This pipeline remains promotion-only, but a failed promotion gate must produce an actionable repair signal instead of a dead-end status. Emit candidate SHA/base, failing job/check/command, relevant artifact/log or review-thread identity, owning surface, required acceptance condition, and proof ceiling. When repository policy allows AFK repair, hand that exact signal to P115 AFK Feedback-Driven Development Loop Executor and keep promotion blocked. The repair owner must create a new exact candidate; re-enter this P105 pipeline from the beginning and never reuse proof from the failed candidate.

12. OBSERVE AND AUDIT THE PIPELINE
Emit a concise workflow summary plus machine-readable promotion receipt containing provider run ID, event/actor, candidate SHA/base identity, required jobs/conclusions, harness receipt identity, E2E receipt/artifacts, promoted artifact identity, target, mutation result, final integration/deployment SHA, and proof ceiling. Logs must make the first failing gate obvious without manual DAG reconstruction.

13. PROVE POST-PROMOTION CONTAINMENT
After push/merge/release/deploy, refresh provider truth. For default-branch integration, verify the proven integration SHA is an ancestor of refreshed default head; do not fail because later valid commits landed. For release/deploy, verify the published/deployed artifact resolves to the proven candidate/artifact identity and required health/smoke checks pass. A queued or accepted command is not successful deployment.

14. STOP AT A BOUNDED FIXED POINT
Inspect the successful run, negative-path runs, permissions, concurrency, trigger filters, artifact lineage, receipts, and post-promotion state once more. Repair concrete holes and rerun affected proof. Stop when one representative promotion path is reproducible, required failures reliably block it, and no practical bypass/stale-proof/race/recursive-writer gap remains. Expand destinations only through explicit scope.

DELIVER
Report promotion graph; canonical commands/workflows; exact-head identity model; harness-vs-application-E2E gates; trigger/dependency design; permissions/concurrency/loop guards; artifact provenance; success and blocking-run evidence; provider run/receipt; post-promotion containment; commit/PR/mainline state; proof ceiling; exact next canary command or authorization blocker. A green YAML syntax check, local-only test run, open PR, or workflow that can write without proving required gates is not completion.

prompts.name: UX Product Designer & Interaction Architect
